transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-03
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Kapoor (Redwood AE), Marc Li (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Epsilon Eng Lead), Tom Rhee (Epsilon CTO), Priya Nair (Epsilon ML Platform), Ben Carter (Epsilon Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Epsilon is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a multi-tenant SaaS product with requirements for 64k+ context, multilingual support (EN/FR/DE/JP), and tool-calling for DB lookups and code execution. Key concerns: latency under 150ms p50 for interactive features, cost per 1M tokens, SOC2/KMS/VPC compliance. Agrees to run a short benchmark and receive security pack and Dedicated worksheet.

Transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Aisha from Redwood, AE on the account. Uh, quick roll call?
[00:07] Tom: Tom here, CTO.
[00:09] Lena: Lena, engineering lead.
[00:11] Priya: Priya, ML platform.
[00:13] Ben: Ben, security.
[00:15] Marc: Marc Li, solutions engineer at Redwood. Great to meet you all.

[00:20] Aisha: Cool. The plan for today is to understand your workload, constraints, and then Marc will walk through architecture options — Hosted, Dedicated, Private — and specifically we wanna dig into model selection, context length, and tool calling. Does that sound good?
[00:33] Tom: Yeah that's perfect. We have a pretty aggressive roadmap so we want to validate feasibility more than a sales pitch right now.

[00:40] Marc: Awesome. Quick clarifying question — are you planning a hybrid flow? Like some endpoints public-hosted and some on VPC for enterprise customers?
[00:48] Priya: Yes, exactly. We have ~60% public user traffic (in-product chat, search), ~40% enterprise tenants who demand VPC and encryption at rest with customer-managed keys. So we'll need a mix.

[00:59] Marc: That kind of mixed topology maps well to Redwood — hosted for low friction, Dedicated for committed capacity and consistent latency, Private/VPC for data-sensitive tenants.

[01:09] Lena: Let's dive into the model side — we are interested in open models because of licensing and cost, but we also care a lot about latency and quality for prompts that include long conversation history — many sessions go to 30k+ tokens and some legal workflows might hit 64k.

[01:22] Marc: Got it. Are those 64k contexts for retrieval-augmented generation or full prompt + doc context?
[01:27] Lena: Mostly RAG — we stream in multiple chunks of documents plus the chat history, so we need a model that can accept large context or we stitch with embeddings and reranker.

[01:34] Marc: Two common patterns: 1) use a long-context model (>=64k) — fewer round trips but higher cost per token; or 2) keep a shorter generation model and do retrieval + reranker/condense step. Both are supported; our runtime supports quantized versions and kernel optimizations to keep latency down.

[01:50] Ben: On the security front, we need SOC2 docs, we use AWS KMS and want to bring our own key in a Private deployment. Also retention: enterprise tenants want 30 to 90 days audit logs, but customer data should be wiped after 30 days. How does Redwood handle that?

[02:03] Aisha: Good question. We provide retention policies at the route level, and for Private we support BYOK via your KMS/HSM. I will send the SOC2 pack and a network diagram for VPC routing.

[02:12] Priya: For model choice, we've been testing a few open models — some Llama-2 and reimplemented variants, also Mistral-like families and some of the new 64k context models from open-source. Latency varies a lot. Can Redwood help compare?

[02:25] Marc: Absolutely. We keep performance profiles for many open models and can run side-by-side benchmarks on Dedicated pools with your prompt sets. Are you mostly optimizing for p50/p95 latency or cost per produced token?

[02:36] Lena: p50 for UI interactions, ideally <150ms for short prompts, while p95 can be higher but we'd prefer <600ms for non-streaming flows. Cost is second but still important.

[02:45] Marc: Short prompts <150ms p50 is ambitious depending on model size and host. For hosted smaller models or quantized LLMs we can hit that at low sequence lengths. For 64k context generation it's harder — we typically see higher latencies because KV cache grows. One approach is to keep the heavy lifting offline and summarize context into a condensed vector or short context before the live generation.

[03:05] Tom: Can we do tool-calling? We want the model to call internal APIs (DB lookups, user permission checks) and potentially run a code execution sandbox for small snippets.

[03:14] Marc: Yes — Redwood supports tool-calling primitives and structured output. We have function calling integrations and can surface tool exec traces in observability. For Private deployments, the tool-call can run in your network to avoid data leakage. Note: you will need a small glue service for auth.

[03:28] Priya: How robust is structured output detection? We rely on strict JSON schemas for downstream processing. Some models hallucinate or miss keys.

[03:34] Marc: We include schema-enforced output layers; we also recommend a two-step verification — model produces a best-effort JSON then a validator layer rejects and retries with stricter prompting. For high-assurance flows, we run a reranker/validate step.

[03:48] Ben: On auditing, if a model triggers a tool call that fetches PII, we need an audit trail and token-level redaction before logs are stored.

[03:55] Marc: Agreed. We can buffer tool-call payloads, apply redaction rules via regex or policy hooks, and then store sanitized traces. Private deployment gives you full control over those traces.

[04:06] Lena: Back to models — what open models do you commonly recommend for multilingual? We need solid EN/FR/DE/JP support, low cost, and ability to fine-tune or do instruction tuning for our domain.

[04:16] Marc: There are a few buckets: 1) Large multilingual models (larger parameter counts) that are strong out-of-the-box but more costly; 2) Smaller models augmented with retrieval and translation pipelines; 3) Specialized instruction-tuned variants. For EN/FR/DE/JP, Mistral and some recent Llama forks have improved coverage. We can run quality evals on your test set to recommend.

[04:36] Priya: We'll share sample transcripts in English and French. Also, we have code snippets, so code gen quality matters. Do you have model families that are better for code + instruction?

[04:45] Marc: Yes. Models trained on code or with code adapters typically do better. We can test code-specific families (e.g., code-LLaMA-ish variants) and measure compilation success rates on a small benchmark.

[04:58] Tom: Pricing model — if we go Dedicated, how does committed capacity map to unit costs? And can we burst?

[05:06] Aisha: Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity with predictable throughput; pricing is based on instance types and committed hours. We do offer burst capacity at controlled rates and can auto-fall back to hosted for overflow. I'll attach a worksheet that shows example math per 1M tokens.

[05:20] Lena: For Dedicated, can we pin specific model versions? We need reproducible outputs for regression testing.

[05:26] Marc: Yes — model pinning and versioned rollouts (canary/A-B) are supported in Dedicated and Private. The console shows token-level diffs and quality monitors tied to prompt sets so you can detect regressions.

[05:40] Priya: How does KV cache behave with 64k contexts? I'm worried about memory blowup on GPU and OOMs.

[05:47] Marc: Good point. The runtime uses segmented KV caching and offloads rarely-used segments; we also support attention kernel selection that trades compute for memory. For extremely long context we recommend a hybrid — keep active context in cache and push older chunks to embeddings store and fetch when needed. For on-prem we can provision high-memory GPUs.

[06:05] Ben: Network topology for VPC — do you require egress to Redwood control plane? Our privacy team wants the control plane in our VPC if possible.

[06:13] Aisha: For Private, you control the control plane; for Dedicated there's a customer-managed VPC peering option so control-plane calls are minimized. We'll send the network diagram and what ports are needed.

[06:24] Marc: Also worth noting that for benchmarks we can simulate your network conditions — test throughput across your region and measure cold start time for model shards.

[06:33] Lena: Ok can we talk about a real example? We have a support product where the flow is: user message (short), system fetches latest 3 articles (about 4k tokens), plus chat history of ~6k tokens, then model generates a short answer — target latency 200ms p50.

[06:49] Marc: For that flow, a mid-sized quantized model with a retrieval/rerank step would probably hit targets. If you want single-shot without retrieval you'd need a long-context model but cost & latency go up. We should benchmark both patterns against your real prompts.

[07:05] Priya: We'll provide a small dataset of 500 typical sessions and token distributions.

[07:10] Aisha: Great — action: Marc will request the dataset; Marc will run a Dedicated benchmark and share results.

[07:16] Marc: I'll also include memory and cost breakdowns — tokens in, tokens out, KV cache growth patterns.

[07:22] Tom: Regarding function/tool calling, one operational question: are tools synchronous? We want guaranteed execution ordering for some flows (e.g., check-permission, then redact, then respond).

[07:33] Marc: You can configure tool calls to be synchronous or async. For synchronous flows we block until tool result returns; we publish logs and trace IDs to the console. For high-throughput flows async is better.

[07:44] Lena: Any caveats with streaming responses and tool-calls? Sometimes streaming plus function calls can be messy.

[07:50] Marc: We support partial streaming with function prelude, but if the tool call changes the generation prompt mid-stream we recommend a replace-and-restart pattern — it's a tradeoff. We'll demo patterns in the follow-up.

[08:03] Ben: About compliance: do you support SAML SSO and role-based RBAC for console access?

[08:09] Aisha: Yes we support SAML/Sso, SCIM provisioning, and granular RBAC. For enterprise we can integrate with your IdP and limit console access.

[08:17] Priya: A question about quantization — do certain models degrade on instruction quality when quantized? We've seen some hallucinations after aggressive quantization.

[08:26] Marc: Right — quantization can affect generation quality. We maintain profiles noting where 8-bit or 4-bit quantization introduces issues. For instruction-heavy tasks we sometimes recommend mixed precision or QAT. We'll surface recommended quantization profiles per model.

[08:40] Tom: Also curious about multi-region failover — if one region saturates, what's the latency penalty to fallback to another region?

[08:48] Marc: Our smart routing can failover, but latency depends on geo distance. We can route to nearest compatible model variant; for critical flows we recommend cross-region Dedicated capacity or an active-passive setup.

[08:59] Lena: Anything to know about cost of embeddings for our RAG flow? We will embed documents and keep an index; is that charged separately?

[09:06] Aisha: Embeddings are billed per-unit; we also offer caching suggestions — if docs seldom change we cache embeddings and reduce repeated compute. Redwood Optimize can recommend embedding dimension/caching strategy to reduce cost.

[09:20] Priya: On evaluation — do you integrate with eval frameworks? We want automated regression alerts on a prompt set.

[09:26] Marc: Yes — Redwood has eval hooks and quality monitors; you can upload prompt sets and we run nightly checks and alert on regressions. The console surfaces token-level diffs so you can see changes in behavior.

[09:38] Ben: Operationally, how do we handle secrets for tool-calls? We have secrets manager in AWS; we can't put keys in plaintext in Redwood logs.

[09:47] Marc: Tool-call secrets are injected at runtime and not stored in plaintext. For Private we keep secret management within your env; for hosted we support transient secrets via vault integrations and redaction.

[09:58] Aisha: Quick pivot — what success metrics will help you decide? Time to production, latency targets, cost per MAU, compliance checklist?

[10:07] Priya: Main metrics: time to production for first tenant (6 weeks ideal), latency p50 <150ms for common flows, cost per 1M tokens under $X (they refrained from giving number), and passing security review with BYOK.

[10:19] Tom: Also, we need model reproducibility and a clear rollback path when model updates cause regressions.

[10:24] Marc: That is built in — version pinning, canaries, automatic fallback to previous model variant if QA fails.

[10:31] Lena: Can Redwood run a short pilot? We want to mirror production traffic for 48 hours on a small Dedicated pool.

[10:39] Marc: Yes we offer pilots — typically a 24–72 hour benchmark on a dedicated pool with your dataset. We'll provide the runner and the results dashboard.

[10:46] Priya: We'll need detailed metrics: per-route latency, token breakdown, memory usage, and function-call counts.

[10:53] Marc: We'll include all of that. Also will provide breakdown by sequence length buckets.

[11:00] Ben: On legal/procurement — we need a standard DPA and we have a vendor questionnaire.

[11:07] Aisha: We'll attach a DPA draft and answers to common vendor questionnaire items; for anything special we'll route to legal.

[11:14] Tom: What about on-prem? Is that realistic for us in the long run? We have strict data residency for some contracts.

[11:21] Marc: On-prem is supported but heavier ops footprint. Private VPC deployments give most of the benefits with lower ops. For full on-prem air-gapped setups we have an on-prem package but it needs more lead time.

[11:33] Lena: One more technical nuance — tokenization differences across model families cause token count variance. Do you normalize when comparing cost?

[11:41] Marc: Yes we normalize by BPE/tokenizer counts in the benchmark and show per-model tokens in/out. That's why we request the raw text samples.

[11:50] Priya: We'll circulate the 500 sessions and two evaluation rubrics: one for conversational correctness, one for code snippets.

[11:56] Aisha: Great. To recap next steps — Aisha will send security pack, Dedicated worksheet, and DPA draft. Marc will request dataset and set up a 24–48 hour benchmark. Epsilon will provide sample prompts and vendor questionnaire answers.

[12:12] Tom: Sounds good. Anything else?
[12:15] Ben: No, thanks.

[12:17] Aisha: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark kickoff and a deeper tool-calling demo.

[12:24] Marc: Thanks all.

[12:26] (call ends)
